newsitem.title: MALI: Malians hope Christopher visit will boost U.S. aid.
newsitem.headline: Malians hope Christopher visit will boost U.S. aid.

text.p: The people of Mali prepared a rousing welcome for U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa on Monday, hoping it would lead to greater American aid to the poor region.
The welcoming party, including traditional dance groups, started taking positions at Bamako airport several hours before Christopher was due to arrive from Israel.
"The visit of the Secretary of State is a tribute to democracy," wrote the government daily L'Essor in an editorial, referring to Mali's smooth break with one-party dictatorship.
"But it can also be expected to be an opportunity for (Mali) to plead for bilateral aid to be maintained at a level compatible with persistent emergencies in Mali," it added.
U.S. officials say Christopher chose Mali for the start of the first visit in six years to sub-Saharan Africa by a U.S. secretary of state to honour Malian democracy.

American diplomacy in West Africa has recently been preoccupied with checking the spread of instability in the region, notably from the six-year-old conflict in Liberia where the United States historiaclly wields the most influence.
Peace in Liberia, Angola, Burundi and the Great Lakes region of Africa are at the heart of the Africa visit.

U.S. officials say Christopher will use the regional tour, which includes visits to Ethiopia, Tanzania, South Africa and Angola, to try and rally Africans behind a U.S. campaign against a new term for U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

Africa is divided over Boutros-Ghali. The Organisation of African Unity summit in Cameroon last July backed the Egyptian officially but made it clear Africa's ultimate concern was that the job should go to an African.
"The visit of Mr Christopher is an occasion for Africa to state its backing for Boutros-Ghali, who already has Mali's support," wrote the independent daily l'Observateur.

Washington's ties with Mali, a nation of 9.4 million people with annual per capita income of $250, have been good since Mali gained independence in 1960. They were strengthened after the first democratically-elected government was installed in 1992.

Assistant Secretary of State George Moose, who specialises in African affairs, said Christopher will "showcase the significant contribution, progress, that Mali has been making in terms of both democratic reform and economic reform".

In addition, Christopher will highlight Mali's "commitment to reconciliation at home and its contribution to regional peacekeeping and stability throughout the sub-region and the region", Moose told reporters.

After his scheduled arrival late on Monday, Christopher was due hold talks on Tuesday with Malian President Alpha Oumar Konare. A meeting is planned with private voluntary organisations and Malian parlimentarians.
Soon after he took office in 1993, Christopher promised that the Clinton administration would make Africa a high priority and give it the attention it deserves.
Officials say Christopher has been unable to get to sub-Saharan Africa until now because of the pressure of other business, including Bosnia and Middle East peace negotiations.

But the timing of the visit just weeks ahead of the November U.S. presidential election could give President Bill Clinton -- already running ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole in public opinion polls -- an extra boost among black voters.
